papers.title_in_file: HOW QUANTUM CAN FUEL OPERATIONAL EXCELLENCE TODAY
papers.what_it_is: A D-Wave marketing ebook (2023) that argues quantum annealing and hybrid solvers are usable for business optimization now, with three customer case snippets (Port of Los Angeles, Pattison Food Group, Recruit Communications).

assertions.value: The authors state that annealing quantum computing uses the principles of quantum mechanics to search for the lowest energy state, which corresponds to the optimal solution of a given problem.
assertions.anchor: Two approaches: quantum annealing and gate model, p.6
quotes: Annealing quantum computing uses the principles of quantum mechanics to search for the lowest energy state, corresponding to the optimal solution of a given problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own approach; no evidence is given in the ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: A one-sentence marketing description. It does not say that the annealer finds the optimum, only that the lowest energy state corresponds to it.

assertions.value: The authors state that annealing quantum computing is particularly well suited for complex combinatorial optimization problems.
assertions.anchor: Two approaches: quantum annealing and gate model, p.6
quotes: It is particularly well suited for complex combinatorial optimization problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's statement about its own product class; no comparison with classical solvers is given.
assertions.reader_inference: No benchmark or classical baseline supports the statement in this ebook.

assertions.value: The authors state that solving complex combinatorial optimization problems can help businesses make better decisions, reduce costs, increase production and design better products, and can help researchers make new scientific discoveries, build better materials and synthesize new medicine.
assertions.anchor: Two approaches: quantum annealing and gate model, p.6
quotes: Solving these problems can help businesses make better decisions, reduce costs, increase production, and design better products.
It can help researchers make new scienti ic discoveries, build better materials, and synthesize new medicine.
assertions.certainty_reason: General promotional benefits with no evidence in the ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints 'scienti ic' for 'scientific' (a lost ligature); the quote keeps the printed form.

assertions.value: The authors describe gate model quantum computing as manipulating individual qubits using quantum gates, analogous to the logic gates in classical computing, implemented with hardware such as superconducting qubits, trapped ions or topological qubits, with targeted applications in materials science, pharmaceutical research and prime factorization.
assertions.anchor: Two approaches: quantum annealing and gate model, p.6
quotes: Gate model quantum computing involves manipulating individual qubits using quantum gates, which are analogous to the logic gates in classical computing.
such as superconducting qubits, trapped ions, or topological qubits.
Targeted applications include materials science, pharmaceutical research and prime factorization.
assertions.certainty_reason: A brief general description by a vendor of annealers, not of gate-model machines.
assertions.reader_inference: The ebook names two approaches as 'the two main approaches', which leaves out other models; the description is the competitor's category as seen by an annealing vendor.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two main approaches to building quantum computers are quantum annealing and gate model.
assertions.anchor: Two approaches: quantum annealing and gate model, p.6
quotes: The two main approaches to building quantum computers are quantum annealing and gate model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsupported framing statement by a vendor.
assertions.reader_inference: The framing is the vendor's; it does not cite a source.

assertions.value: The authors state that gate model quantum computers are largely being used for small scale problems and lab research, while D-Wave's annealing quantum computers are already being used in production for business applications.
assertions.anchor: Two approaches: quantum annealing and gate model, p.6
quotes: While gate model quantum computers are largely being used for small scale problems and lab research, D-Wave’s annealing quantum computers are already being used in production for business applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's statement about its own product use; supported only by the three case snippets in the same ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: 'In production' is not defined in the ebook; it does not say that production use shows a quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum-hybrid applications bring together quantum and classical computation to solve highly complex computational problems.
assertions.anchor: Enter hybrid solvers, p.7
quotes: Quantum-hybrid applications bring together quantum and classical computation to solve highly complex computational problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own hybrid approach.
assertions.reader_inference: The ebook does not say which part of a hybrid run is quantum and which is classical; the diagram on the same page carries only the labels 'BUSINESS APPLICATION', 'HYBRID' and 'Classical Computing' in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that by automatically allocating the best resource, hybrid solvers can achieve better performance for real-world problems with hundreds of thousands of variables and huge numbers of potential solutions.
assertions.anchor: Enter hybrid solvers, p.7
quotes: By automatically allocating the best resource, hybrid solvers can achieve better performance for real-world problems with hundreds of thousands of variables and huge numbers of potential solutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's statement about its own product with no measurement or baseline in the ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Better performance' has no stated comparison, metric or size. The ebook does not say what share of the work runs on quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that hybrid solvers are available over the cloud and abstract the underlying quantum system, so users can specify their problems in business terms and more easily start developing quantum applications.
assertions.anchor: Enter hybrid solvers, p.7
quotes: Available over the cloud, hybrid solvers also abstract the underlying quantum system. This enables users to specify their problems in business terms and more easily get started on developing quantum applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own service.

assertions.value: The authors state that their approach is practical: they facilitate applying current problem-solving knowledge to a hybrid platform so that customers can increasingly use quantum power.
assertions.anchor: Enter hybrid solvers, p.7
quotes: Our approach is practical: we facilitate applying current problem-solving knowledge to a hybrid platform so customers can increasingly use quantum power.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's statement of its own approach.

assertions.value: The authors state that qubits can simultaneously be in multiple states, called superposition, and that superposition allows quantum computers to perform computations on many possibilities at once.
assertions.anchor: What is different about quantum computing?, p.5
quotes: Qubits can simultaneously be in multiple states, called superposition. Superposition allows quantum computers to perform computations on many possibilities at once.
assertions.certainty_reason: A popular-level statement without a proof or a condition.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the common popular simplification. Superposition alone does not give a speed-up, because a measurement returns one outcome; the ebook gives no condition under which an advantage holds.

assertions.value: The authors state that superposition and other quantum effects enable quantum computers to excel at solving complex problems, sometimes faster and more efficiently than classical computers.
assertions.anchor: What is different about quantum computing?, p.5
quotes: Superposition and other quantum effects enable quantum computers to excel at solving complex problems, sometimes faster and more efficiently than classical computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsupported general claim; the word 'sometimes' leaves its scope open.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim is hedged ('sometimes'); the ebook does not name the problems or the baselines.

assertions.value: The authors describe classical computers as using bits, representing one square of a landscape at a time and solving a problem by stepping from square to square in search of the lowest point, and describe solving a hard computational problem as searching a space of possible solutions.
assertions.anchor: What is different about quantum computing?, p.5
quotes: Solving a hard computational problem requires searching a space of possible solutions.
A classical computer can represent one square at a time, and it solves problems by stepping from square to square in search of the lowest point.
assertions.certainty_reason: A pedagogical analogy, not a technical statement.
assertions.reader_inference: The analogy describes a local-descent search. Classical optimizers include methods that do not step square by square (for example, simulated annealing with restarts, or branch and bound), so the analogy is not a fair description of the classical state of the art.

assertions.value: The authors report that industry research found problem complexity was a major obstacle to solving computationally-dependent business problems, cited by almost 30% of those surveyed, and that 39% of companies abandoned the effort to solve those particular problems.
assertions.anchor: Problems are getting more complex, p.3
quotes: Industry research revealed that problem complexity was a major obstacle to solving computationally-dependent business problems, cited by almost 30% of the surveyed.
As a result, 39% of companies abandoned the effort to solve those particular problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A survey result with no named source, date or sample in the ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: The 'industry research' is not named, dated or sized in the ebook. It is not clear that the 39% share is of the same respondents as the 30% share.

assertions.value: The authors state that many problems are so hard that classical computers cannot keep up, either because solutions take too long or because the computational power needed is lacking, and that greater amounts of power are required for even minimal speed gains, resulting in sustainability and environmental concerns.
assertions.anchor: Traditional computing can't keep up, p.3
quotes: Many problems are so hard that classical computers can’t keep up
either solutions take too long or, in many cases, they lack the computational power needed to solve the problem at all.
Greater amounts of power are required for even minimal speed gains, resulting in sustainability and environmental concerns.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general vendor claim with no evidence or named problem in the ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: The quote omits the em dash that joins the two clauses in the source; the value joins them with 'either ... or'.

assertions.value: The authors report that a Hyperion Research report showed that over 80% of enterprises surveyed are looking to move forward with their quantum computing efforts with increased funding and resources.
assertions.anchor: The quantum era in business has begun, p.9
quotes: A report from Hyperion Research showed that over 80% of enterprises surveyed are looking to move forward with their quantum computing efforts with increased funding and resources.
assertions.certainty_reason: A third-party survey result relayed by a vendor; the report, its date and its sample are not given.
assertions.reader_inference: No sample size, survey date, report title or selection of respondents is given. Respondents who answered a quantum survey may already be interested in quantum computing.

assertions.value: The authors report that one-third of the surveyed enterprises are aggressively looking to incorporate quantum computing into their overall computing environment.
assertions.anchor: The quantum era in business has begun, p.9
quotes: One-third are aggressively looking to incorporate quantum computing into their overall computing environment.
assertions.certainty_reason: A third-party survey result relayed by a vendor; no sample or date is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer does not say whether 'One-third' refers to the over-80% group or to all respondents.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computing early adopters see the promise of quantum computing for a wide range of computational workloads, including machine learning applications, finance-oriented optimization, and logistics/supply chain management.
assertions.anchor: The quantum era in business has begun, p.9
quotes: Quantum computing (QC) early adopters see the promise of QC for a wide range of computational workloads, including machine learning applications, finance-oriented optimization, and logistics/supply chain management.
assertions.certainty_reason: A survey finding about adopter expectations, relayed without detail.
assertions.reader_inference: This reports what adopters expect, not what quantum computers have been shown to do for these workloads.

assertions.value: The authors report that the most important driver for quantum adoption in the survey was the need to overcome business challenges to achieve faster and more efficient operations as a means of saving cost and improving customer satisfaction, and that also cited were making complex data-driven decisions faster and more accurately and maintaining a competitive edge in a rapidly changing technological landscape.
assertions.anchor: The quantum era in business has begun, p.9
quotes: The most important was the need to overcome business challenges to achieve faster and more efficient operations as a means of saving cost and improving customer satisfaction.
Also cited were the ability to make complex data-driven decisions faster and more accurately, and the need to maintain their competitive edge in a rapidly changing technological landscape.
assertions.certainty_reason: A survey result relayed by a vendor without sample or percentages.
assertions.reader_inference: No percentages are given for the drivers.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computing is still in its early stages, and that many companies are racing ahead, enhancing operational efficiency and reducing costs.
assertions.anchor: Section after hybrid solvers, p.8
quotes: While quantum computing is still in its early stages, many companies are racing ahead, enhancing operational efficiency and reducing costs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general vendor statement; the efficiency and cost claims are not backed by data beyond the three case snippets.
assertions.reader_inference: The ebook itself states that the field is early stage; this limits how far its case snippets generalise.

assertions.value: The authors state that hybrid solvers are being used by companies from diverse industries, many achieving remarkable results.
assertions.anchor: Enter hybrid solvers, p.7
quotes: Hybrid solvers are being used by companies from diverse industries, many achieving remarkable results.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's statement about its own customers' use, with no data.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Remarkable results' is not defined.

assertions.value: The authors state that D-Wave's quantum system has been used as part of the SavantX HONE optimization engine at the Port of Los Angeles, with the goal of expediting delivery of containers out of the terminal while increasing the amount of cargo that can be handled.
assertions.anchor: Case study: logistics, SavantX and the Port of Los Angeles, p.12
quotes: D-Wave’s quantum system has been used as part of the SavantX HONE optimization engine at the Port of Los Angeles.
The goal was to expedite delivery of containers out of the terminal while increasing the amount of cargo that can be handled.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of a customer deployment.
assertions.reader_inference: The ebook does not say which QPU or solver was used, which part of HONE ran on it, or how large the problem was.

assertions.value: The authors state that in 2021 alone the equivalent of more than 10 million twenty-foot container units were transferred from ships to trucks at the Port of Los Angeles, and that optimizing how containers are sorted, sequenced and delivered by as little as a few percentage points can translate into tens of millions of dollars a year.
assertions.anchor: Case study: logistics, Optimizing logistics at the Port of LA, p.12
quotes: In 2021 alone, the equivalent of more than 10 million twenty-foot container units were transferred from ships to the trucks that convey them to their inland destinations.
Optimizing how containers are sorted, sequenced, and delivered at the port by as little as a few percentage points can translate into tens of millions of dollars a year.
assertions.certainty_reason: A figure stated without a source in the ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: The throughput and dollar figures have no cited source.

assertions.value: The authors quote the SavantX Team as saying that with HONE and D-Wave each huge crane handled 60% more cargo per day while the turnaround time for trucks was reduced by 12%.
assertions.anchor: Case study: logistics, Optimizing logistics at the Port of LA, p.12
quotes: “With HONE and D-Wave, each huge crane handled 60% more cargo per day, while the turnaround time for trucks was reduced by 12%.”
MORE CARGO HANDLED EACH DAY PER CRANE
assertions.certainty_reason: A partner's quoted outcome with no baseline, period, method or independent check in the ebook.
assertions.reader_inference: The ebook gives no baseline, time period or measurement method, and does not separate the effect of HONE from that of the D-Wave system, or of the quantum part of the hybrid from the classical part. It is not evidence of a quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that until recently it took Pattison Food Group 80 person-hours of work to build out the schedule for its delivery drivers each week, because developing the schedules needed to consider a large number of variables and constraints.
assertions.anchor: Case study: e-commerce, Optimizing driver scheduling, p.14
quotes: Until recently, it took Pattison Food Group (PFG) 80 person-hours of work to build out the schedule for its delivery drivers each week, as developing schedules needed to consider a large number of variables and constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: A customer baseline relayed by a vendor without a source or method.

assertions.value: The authors state that PFG is using D-Wave's quantum-hybrid technology to automate delivery schedules, preferences and history, and policies, and that the weekly efforts for initial scheduling creation were reduced by ~80% within the first three months.
assertions.anchor: Case study: e-commerce, Optimizing driver scheduling, p.14
quotes: Now PFG is using D-Wave’s quantum-hybrid technology to automate delivery schedules, preferences and history, and policies.
As a result, the weekly efforts for initial scheduling creation were reduced by ~80% within the first three months.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor-reported customer result with no method, baseline detail or independent check.
assertions.reader_inference: The reduction is in staff time to create a schedule. The ebook does not compare against a classical automated scheduler, so the saving may come from automation and not from the quantum part.

assertions.value: The authors quote the Manager of Analytics Development at PFG as saying that PFG will be the first grocery chain to actually use quantum computing to serve its business needs.
assertions.anchor: Case study: e-commerce, Optimizing driver scheduling, p.14
quotes: “We will be the first grocery chain to actually use quantum computing to serve our business needs.”
—Manager of Analytics Development at PFG
assertions.certainty_reason: A customer's forward-looking statement quoted by a vendor.
assertions.reader_inference: A statement of intent, not a result.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because there are a finite number of time-slots in a day's programming and multiple advertisers who may run several different ads, placing TV ads for maximum exposure is a highly complex combinatorial optimization problem.
assertions.anchor: Case study: marketing and branding, Maximizing brand reach, p.16
quotes: Since there are a finite number of time-slots in the course of a day’s programming and multiple advertisers who may run several different ads, this is a highly complex combinatorial optimization problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's problem description with no formulation or size given.
assertions.reader_inference: No variable count, constraint set or formulation is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that recent work by Recruit Group on optimizing the timing of TV ads using D-Wave's quantum hybrid solver was so successful that it is now being used in production to determine when these broadcast ads run.
assertions.anchor: Case study: marketing and branding, Maximizing brand reach, p.16
quotes: Recent work on optimizing the timing of TV ads using D-Wave’s quantum hybrid solver was so successful, it is now being used in production to determine when these broadcast ads run.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor-reported customer outcome with no data, baseline or metric of success.
assertions.reader_inference: 'So successful' has no stated metric. The ebook gives no comparison with the previous or a classical method.

assertions.value: The authors quote Recruit Communications as saying that the most exciting part of the project is that millions of people in Japan watch TV commercials optimized by the D-Wave quantum machine.
assertions.anchor: Case study: marketing and branding, Maximizing brand reach, p.16
quotes: “I think the most exciting part of this project is that millions of people in Japan watch TV commercials optimized by the D-Wave quantum machine.”
assertions.certainty_reason: A customer's quoted remark; reach is not a performance measure.
assertions.reader_inference: The quote describes audience size, not an improvement over a baseline.

assertions.value: The authors state that D-Wave offers resources for business and technical people, including case stories, technical white papers, open source code and documentation, and free access to D-Wave's Leap quantum cloud service, and that they offer a complimentary 30-minute quantum consultation for businesses.
assertions.anchor: Resources for business and technical leaders, p.18; We can help, p.19
quotes: Open source code and documentation
Free access to D-Wave’s Leap™ quantum cloud service
we offer a complimentary 30-minute quantum consultation for businesses.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's statement of its own offerings in a 2023 ebook; offerings can change.
assertions.reader_inference: The terms of the free access are not stated in the ebook and may have changed since 2023.

assertions.value: The ebook presents no experiment, benchmark, classical baseline, proof or methodology of its own; its results are customer case snippets and a third-party survey relayed by the vendor.
assertions.anchor: Whole document, pp.1-19
quotes: Quantum computers can help transform business challenges into business advantage.

Hybrid solvers are being used by companies from diverse industries, many achieving remarkable results. This is a gamechanger for businesses who want to unlock the computational power of quantum computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: A reader's characterization of the document's evidential status, supported by the vendor's framing quotes.
assertions.reader_inference: Every number in the ebook is either from an unnamed survey, a customer quote, or an unreferenced vendor figure. It is a marketing document and weak evidence for any quantum advantage.
